paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few problems in science combine such obvious importance with such stubborn resistance as the problem of consciousness. We know a great deal about how the brain processes information: how light is converted into signals, how memories are stored and how decisions are made. What we cannot say is why any of this processing should be accompanied by experience, by the felt quality of seeing red or the ache of a bruise. The philosopher David Chalmers called this the hard problem, to distinguish it from the easier, though still formidable, questions about brain function.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Many neuroscientists regard the distinction as a confusion. Their position holds that once we explain all the functions of the brain, including our tendency to report that we are conscious, nothing remains to be explained. Consciousness, on this view, resembles the vitalism of earlier centuries: people once believed that life required a special force, until biochemistry explained living things without it. I find the analogy suggestive but not conclusive, for the cases differ in one crucial respect. Life was defined by observable functions such as growth and reproduction; consciousness is defined, at least in part, by experience that is available only to the one who has it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Other researchers pursue a middle course. Theories such as integrated information theory propose that consciousness corresponds to a particular mathematical property of a system, and attempt to measure it. Others, such as global workspace theory, link consciousness to the broadcasting of information across the brain. These approaches have generated testable predictions and valuable experiments, for example on patients who appear unresponsive yet show brain activity when asked to imagine playing tennis. Whatever their ultimate fate, they demonstrate that the study of consciousness is no longer the preserve of philosophers.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Still, I doubt that empirical progress alone will dissolve the hard problem. Correlating brain states with reports of experience tells us where and when consciousness occurs, not why it exists. A complete map of such correlations would be an extraordinary achievement, and might allow us to predict what a person experiences, but a prediction is not an explanation. We may therefore have to expand our conception of explanation itself, in the way physics did when it accepted that fields and forces, which are not directly visible, are fundamental features of the world.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The question has practical urgency. If we cannot say what makes a system conscious, we cannot confidently say which systems are. Animals, newborn infants, patients in vegetative states and, increasingly, artificial intelligence all raise the issue. A cautious ethic would err on the side of respect: to treat a system as conscious when it is not may be wasteful, but to treat a conscious one as an object would be a serious wrong.
